title: Quantum non-local games: Quantum relations, projection lattices and rule operators
abstract: Quantum non-local games with quantum inputs or outputs have been formulated in several different languages, including rank-one and quantum XOR games, support maps between projection lattices, probabilistic quantum hypergraphs, and Frobenius-algebraic rule operators on finite quantum sets. We give a unified operator-algebraic comparison of these models by assigning to each rule its winning transformation space: the operator space of transformations accepted with certainty. We introduce \(\mathcal R\)-projection-test quantum games with finite-dimensional input and output von Neumann algebras and an arbitrary, possibly infinite-dimensional, referee von Neumann algebra \(\mathcal R\). Their winning transformation spaces are precisely operator spaces with a natural bimodule structure, equivalently rectangular quantum relations. We compare this formalism with projection-lattice games, hypergraph quantum games, and the graphical rule-operator definition. Projection-lattice games capture exactly the reflexive winning bimodules. Hypergraph quantum games admit value-preserving projection-test realisations, and, after passing to perfect transformations, describe the same reflexive part as projection-lattice games. Using Daws' technique, we also translate rule operators to projections in tensor products of finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras. This identification places graphical rules in the same operator-bimodule framework and preserves both values and perfectness. Finally, we compare concurrency with the synchronicity conditions of Goldberg and of Bochniak--Kasprzak--Sołtan. The framework is illustrated by classical, rank-one, quantum XOR, colouring, and quantum graph homomorphism and isomorphism games.
summary: This paper unifies multiple mathematical descriptions of quantum non-local games—including those based on projection lattices, hypergraphs, and rule operators—into a single operator-algebraic framework. By identifying the 'winning transformation space' as the central object, the authors show that these disparate models describe the same underlying mathematical structure. This provides a powerful, consistent theoretical tool for analyzing quantum correlations and non-locality.
main_problem: The paper aims to systematically compare various mathematical formalisms used to describe quantum non-local games and establish a unified operator-algebraic framework for them.
main_result: The winning strategies across diverse game models (projection-lattice, hypergraph, rule operators) are unified by the concept of an operator bimodule, with projection-lattice games capturing the reflexive part of this structure.
method: The authors use operator algebra techniques, defining the 'winning transformation space' as the central object of comparison across different game definitions.
model_or_system: The core model is the quantum non-local game, involving separated players and a referee, formalized using input/output von Neumann algebras and projection test structures.
key_observables: The winning transformation space (an operator bimodule), the game value (probability), and the property of 'perfectness' of a strategy.
important_parameters: The structure of the input/output von Neumann algebras ($X, Y, A, B$) and the referee algebra ($\mathcal{R}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis extends to arbitrary, possibly infinite-dimensional, referee von Neumann algebras ($\mathcal{R}$), and relies on comparing the 'reflexive' parts of the various formalisms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes the main quantum-game formalisms compared, including Projection-lattice, Rule operator, and Hypergraph quantum games.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the prototypical projection-test game, then systematically comparing its winning space to those derived from projection-lattice games, hypergraph games, and rule operators, culminating in comparisons of concurrency conditions.
why_interesting: While the topic is abstract quantum information theory, the rigorous mathematical framework connecting different physical models (like graph homomorphisms) to a single algebraic structure is highly relevant for developing general theoretical tools in quantum physics.
